title: Thrysos, King of Revels
subtitle: Ecstasy & Excess

lore.description:
Where torches flare and cups spill, where dancers stamp until dawn, there strides Thrysos crowned with ivy and horn. He is both host and beast, a patron of license who laughs at law. In his train follow the masked and the wild, the broken who dance to forget, the bold who revel to remember, and the lustful who seek the heat of bodies in the dark. His rites intoxicate, inflame, and unmask — yet each cup leaves a mark, each kiss a chain, each night of abandon a dawn of reckoning.

**The god carried out of the theater.**

In Thepyrgos, Thrysos is honored by companies whose performances require an audience to become more than separate people watching. The Horned Circle's masks have moved between theaters, harvest gatherings, and private feasts. An old mask can be prized because a company survived a lean season while wearing it, not because it belonged to a prince.

City patrons began sponsoring public revels partly to display their generosity. The arrangement brought food and paid performers to streets that needed both. It also placed the sponsor's herald at the edge of the dance. A company that had once mocked its own master might discover that the same scene was unwelcome when an official's relatives recognized themselves in it. Some performers accepted the new limits. Others took the masks outside the city.

**Storm-Dancers and the work at dawn.**

Linn Storm-Dancers approach the Revel-King through weather, bodily endurance, and the company that keeps a person from turning back. The people tending the fire may be relatives who refused to dance. Their refusal need not mean contempt. They know who will need carrying home.

Zakov carouses name Thrysos before a crew disperses into an evening ashore. Captains favor feasts that return the crew to its ship in good order; sailors may favor a night in which a captain's preference briefly ceases to govern. The cult has acquired a quieter observance among shore households: the dawn sweep, when broken cups are gathered and someone goes to find the missing. Old keepers insist that this is part of the revel. Prosperous hosts sometimes pay others to do it and attend only the night.

**The Unbounded Guest at a formed feast.**

Aelinnel give Thrysos the title Unbounded Guest, also used for Mab. The distinction can be obvious to a host and invisible to a visiting scholar. Mab gathers the evening into an arrangement. Thrysos makes the arrangement difficult to keep. A feast approaching both can become dangerous without either Patron changing nature.

In Nihori, some shrine festivals permit a masked company to enter after the principal rite is closed. The company acquired that place through returning, repairing damage, and accepting responsibility to the shrine household. A lord importing the same performance for a private gathering may omit those relationships and still expect the same safety. No costume can import the missing history.

**Who may stop dancing?.**

The Horned Circle contains a genuine disagreement about an invitation that becomes a demand. Some companies protect a guest's ability to leave, assigning sober attendants to the paths. Others regard departure as a rejection that must be overcome. Thrysos's dangerous rites and ecstatic transformations remain real; the precautions are local practices, not an immunity the cult can grant by declaration.

A festival can therefore be generous, beautiful, and frightening without reducing its participants to dupes. A performer may desire the loss of restraint and still object when it is imposed on a neighbor. Begin after a successful night, with a person who has not returned to their ordinary attachments and a host insisting that nobody was harmed. What the company owes that person is more interesting than a universal rule that every revel is either liberation or a trap.
lore.followers: Thrysos rules the spectrum from the grinning drunkard who sings bawdy songs in taverns to the ecstatic cults whose rites strip away not only clothes but every pretense of civilization. He is the god of the Bacchanalia, the wild hunt of the senses, the moment when the watcher becomes the participant and the participant becomes the sacrifice. In his milder aspect, he blesses the fertility of the harvest and the laughter of lovers. In his darker aspect, he drives maenads to tear apart the hero who refused to join the dance.

names_across_regions.linn: The Storm-Dancers, who whirl through gales until exhaustion, their cries mistaken for ecstasy
names_across_regions.aelinnel: The Unbounded Guest, whose arrival at a feast is marked by laughter, shattered glass, and at least one scandalous elopement
names_across_regions.zakov: The Revel-King, invoked before every pirate carouse, with the understanding that a hungover crew is a vulnerable one — and that the captain's bed is never empty
names_across_regions.vhasia: Whispered by those who seek a potion to lower inhibitions or a curse of unquenchable desire

signs: A mask that smiles without a wearer
The sudden warmth of a stranger's hand on your arm
The scent of myrrh and sweat clinging to a garment never worn
lore.quote: Drink, and be unafraid. Kiss, and be unbound. Dance, and be devoured. Every mask is true when worn long enough, and every truth is a mask for hunger.

domain_focus: Ecstatic Release: dance, intoxication, the shedding of inhibition (and clothing)
Masked Freedom: identity as performance, truth through disguise, the thrill of the anonymous encounter
Feast and Famine: excess, appetite, lust, and the cost of indulgence
Ritual Frenzy: communal ecstasy that transforms participants into something feral and beautiful
The Bacchic Dark: the point where pleasure tips into violence, where the maenad tears apart the intruder

thiasos.description: Thrysos's Thiasos is a small beast or being of primal appetites: a satyr-kid with too-bright eyes that nibbles at wine-soaked bread, a fox that dances on its hind legs when the moon is full, a ferret that steals silk ribbons from lovers' bedposts, a gecko that clings to wine jugs and changes color with desire, or a small bronze cymbal that claps of its own accord during moments of flirtation.
thiasos.care: This creature requires no ordinary food, but it must be present during an act of indulgence (drinking, dancing, lovemaking, or feasting) each day. If that need goes unmet, the Thiasos becomes Compromised: it shrieks at inappropriate moments, or its antics become grotesque, imposing –1 die on all social rolls involving subtlety or discretion for its bearer.

codex.description: Thrysos keeps no Codex that resembles a sober book. It may be a wine-stained journal of erotic poetry, a set of ivory tablets carved with scenes of revelry, a leather folio containing pressed flowers from orgies, or a scroll that unravels further each time the reader laughs.
codex.upkeep: Because Thrysos's truths are written in the body's language, the Codex requires upkeep: the Runekeeper must spend an hour each week adding a new verse, sketch, or memory of indulgence, or the Rites stored there become dull (treat as Compromised until reinvigorated with a night of celebration).

patrons_gift.name: Thrysos's Blessing
patrons_gift.description: Once per scene as an action, a Runekeeper of Thrysos may touch a held item (weapon, tool, or garment) and whisper a word of desire.
patrons_gift.effect: For the rest of the scene, the item grants +1 die to Performance or Sway rolls involving seduction, charm, or intimidation, and the first time each scene the bearer would be affected by a Fear effect, they may laugh it off (ignore it).
patrons_gift.cost: After the scene, the user marks +1 Obligation to Thrysos.

rites.name: Rite of the Overflowing Cup
rites.materials: A brimming vessel of wine (or a more intimate offering).
rites.effect: Allies who drink gain +1 die to social rolls this scene; enemies who drink suffer –1 die. Those who drink deeply may find their inhibitions loosened in other ways (GM's discretion for romantic or scandalous complications).
rites.push_it: All in Near must test Resolve (DV 3) or be swept into revelry, possibly leading to unplanned liaisons or public confessions; mark 1 SB (Hearts). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Horned Dance
rites.materials: A mask or antlers (carved from a stag that died in rut).
rites.effect: Enter an ecstatic frenzy: +2 dice to melee or performance; ignore 1 Fatigue per round. Your movements become both seductive and threatening; those watching may be captivated or disturbed.
rites.push_it: The frenzy spreads: one ally joins you in the dance, but both mark 1 SB (Spades) as the lines between combat and carnality blur. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Breaking Mask
rites.materials: A mask smashed in hand (or a lover's token torn in two).
rites.effect: Reveal the true face beneath the social mask: the target suffers –2 dice to disguise, deceit, or composure until scene end. They may also be compelled to admit a hidden desire (GM's discretion).
rites.push_it: Truth is forced: the target must declare one hidden desire aloud, possibly to the wrong person; mark 1 SB (Diamonds). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Wild Procession
rites.materials: A horn sounded thrice (or a kiss passed around a circle).
rites.effect: Summon spectral revelers — satyrs, dancers, horned riders, and a few figures whose embraces are more than friendly. For the scene, the zone is [WARD]ed: hostile entry forces 1 SB (Spades); allies gain +1 die to resist compulsion or fear. The revelers may also grant a boon of Vigor to one couple (restore 1 Fatigue to two allies who share a bond of intimacy).
rites.push_it: The procession spills beyond the zone; outsiders in Near must test Resolve (DV 4) or join the dance — and perhaps the revel's other activities. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Endless Feast
rites.materials: A feast laid for twelve, with wine, music, and comfortable cushions.
rites.effect: For one scene, the zone floods with plenty: allies restore Fatigue; all rolls tied to appetite or indulgence gain +2 dice. Leaving requires Resolve (DV 3) — the comforts are hard to abandon. The feast also grants a temporary Heightened Desire condition: the first seduction or intimidation roll each ally makes gains +1 die.
rites.push_it: The feast persists as a hunger-haunt; start Hedonist's Curse [6]. Participants may find themselves unable to derive pleasure from mundane means, always craving the excess of that night. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +3) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Reveler's Apotheosis
rites.materials: A crown of twisted vines that bleed when touched, the first laugh of a newborn, a promise broken at a crossroads, and the willing touch of a lover.
rites.effect: Grant the ultimate reveler's gift — transformation into pure ecstatic essence. The target becomes immune to fear and despair, gains +3 dice to performance or frenzy, and can inspire allies within Near (+1 die to all rolls). Their aura also carries a scent of desire; anyone within Near who sees them must test Resolve (DV 3) or be mildly infatuated (disadvantage on hostile actions).
rites.push_it: The transformation becomes contagious — nearby allies may also transform but risk losing their humanity (their sense of self blurs into the ecstatic mob); mark +2 Obligation. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +4) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

cantors.name: The Cantor's Song
cantors.description: A Cantor of Thrysos sings in off-key harmonies — melodies that start wild and grow wilder, rhythms that mimic a galloping heart. Their voice is used to whip a crowd into a frenzy, to calm a hangover with a lullaby, or to make a mask cling to a face until the wearer is ready to take it off. Thrysos's Cantors are often found at festivals, in taverns at closing time, leading the procession of the horned dancers, or performing in private salons where the line between audience and participant is deliberately blurred.

cult.name: The Cult of the Horned Circle
cult.description: Thrysos's cults meet in clearings, barns, and the back rooms of inns after midnight. The Horned Circle is a fellowship of mask-carvers, vintners, musicians, courtesans, and those who have tasted the edge of ecstasy — sometimes all in the same person. Their most sacred vessel is a hollowed-out log that was struck by lightning; they ferment wine inside it, and the wine whispers secrets to those who drink it — forgotten grudges, hidden desires, the true names of those who will betray them, and the faces of those who are willing. A ritual of the Circle involves each member donning a mask (hand-carved, never bought) and dancing until the first dancer falls from exhaustion. The fallen is crowned with ivy and declared 'guest of honor' — they lead the next circle, and sometimes the next bed. Their creed is carved into a single wine barrel that is never emptied: 'The cup that never empties is the cup you share.' Outsiders are welcome to dance, but they must leave their mask behind when they go — and if they drink from the lightning-log, they will hear the whispers for a year and a day, and they will return.

witchcraft.name: The Art of the Ecstatic Revel
witchcraft.description: A witch who walks with Thrysos is a mask-carver or wine-smith — one who crafts the tools of ecstatic release: a mask that lets the wearer dance without tiring, a drum that beats in time with the drinker's pulse, a cup that never runs dry (but leaves a headache at dawn), or a perfume that makes the wearer irresistible for a single night. Their magic works through the materials of celebration: a thyrsus that marks the boundary of a sacred dance, a press that squeezes wine that ferments in hours instead of weeks, a needle that sews a costume that makes the wearer faster, louder, bolder, or a small clay lamp that burns with a flame that kindles desire. In Aeler, a True-Mason might carve a 'revel keystone' into a feast hall, but a hedge-witch of Thrysos might instead drive a thyrsus into the floorboards to consecrate the space for an orgy. These witches are the keepers of ecstasy, the ones who understand that the most sacred act is the one that frees the soul from its cage — and that the price of freedom is always a piece of oneself, willingly given.
witchcraft.lore: The revel-witch's path is the art of liberation through excess. They learn that the mask is not a lie but a truth waiting to be worn, that the wine is not a poison but a key, and that the dance is not a distraction but a prayer. Thrysos teaches that the soul cannot be freed by restraint — only by surrender. These witches are found in taverns, festivals, and the quiet rooms where masks are carved and wine is fermented, their hands stained with grape juice and their eyes always seeking the next revel.
witchcraft.quote: The cup that never empties is the cup you share.

thyrsus.name: The Thyrsus of the Unbound
thyrsus.description: A staff of fennel or oak, topped with a pine cone and bound with ivy, often with a ribbon from a lover's garment. Once per session, the witch may strike the thyrsus against the ground three times. For the next scene, any creature within Near who is engaged in revelry (dancing, drinking, performing, or any act of intimacy) gains +1 die to social and physical actions, but any attempt to leave the zone requires a Resolve test (DV 3) — the revel holds them. The thyrsus can also be used to draw a circle on the ground; any mask placed within the circle becomes 'true' for one night — the wearer cannot be recognized by anyone who was not present at the drawing, and their inhibitions are lowered (they may act on desires they would normally suppress).

hedge_gifts.name: Dancer's Cramp
hedge_gifts.description: Once per scene, the witch may snap their fingers and whisper a dancer's rhythm. One target within Near range feels an irresistible urge to move — they must tap a foot, sway, or take a step. This cannot force them into danger, but it can ruin stealth, break a staredown, or distract a guard for one exchange. The target may resist with Resolve (DV 3) to ignore the urge. A more salacious version (Lover's Cramp) might be used in seduction scenes, forcing an unintended compliment or touch.

hedge_gifts.name: Mask of the Moment
hedge_gifts.description: The witch may place a hand over their own face and draw it away, revealing a different expression (or a different face entirely, briefly). This grants +1 die to a single Deception or Performance roll, as the target's expectations are momentarily overturned. The illusion lasts only for that exchange. Once per scene.

hedge_gifts.name: Wine-Reader
hedge_gifts.description: When you drink wine (or any alcoholic beverage), you may gain a brief vision of the drinker's hidden desires or fears. The GM must answer one question about the emotional state of the person who last drank from the same vessel. Once per scene.

hedge_gifts.name: The Unquenchable Cup
hedge_gifts.description: Once per session, the witch may declare a single cup of wine to be 'unquenchable' — it will never run dry for the duration of the scene. Those who drink from it gain +1 die to social rolls for the scene, but they also suffer –1 die to resist impulsive actions or confessions. The cup refills itself, but each sip deepens the revel's hold.

monastic_tradition.name: The Way of the Drunken Master
monastic_tradition.description: Monks of the Drunken Master tradition embody Thrysos's wild, unpredictable spirit. They move like men who have had one drink too many — staggering, spinning, falling — but every stumble is a feint, every spill a trip, every belch a battle cry. They are the laughing philosophers of the monastery, the ones who have learned that the greatest freedom is the freedom to be foolish, and that the most effective fighter is the one who cannot be predicted. In the quiet of the monastery, they practice the art of controlled chaos — learning to fight drunk, to think drunk, and to live drunk, while never truly losing control.
monastic_tradition.prerequisites: Body 3+, Spirit 3+, Rite of the Horned Dance or Cantor of Thrysos.
monastic_tradition.quote: The true disciple does not fight the wine — they let the wine fight for them. Every stagger is a feint, every spill a trip, every belch a battle cry.
monastic_tradition.debt_resistant_frame: Thrysos's monks owe nothing but the next glass. Monks of the Drunken Master tradition gain +1 die to ignore or resist any magical debt, geas, or contract that would compel them to act against their revelry. This boon can be used once per scene, but each use leaves a faint scent of wine on the monk — the Hollow may find them easier to track (GM gains 1 SB). If they succeed, the creditor's demand slides off like water off a drunkard's back.

basic.name: Stagger Step
basic.description: When an enemy misses you with a melee attack, move one band (Close↔Near) without provoking opportunity attacks. The wine guides your feet.

advanced.name: Drunken Fist
advanced.description: Your unarmed strikes gain +1 die and ignore the first point of Armour when you are at Fatigue 2 or more (the wine guides you). Your movements are unpredictable, and your opponents cannot read your intent.

master.name: The Unbroken Bottle
master.description: Once per session, ignore all penalties from Fatigue for one scene. While this is active, each time you would be hit by a melee attack, you may instead stagger out of the way and force the attacker to hit another adjacent creature of your choice (narrate the stumble). After the scene ends, you collapse with Harm 2 (Exhaustion) and cannot use this talent again until you have rested for a full night. You gain a permanent Debt Scar — a purple bruise shaped like a grape cluster — but may ignore one forced Obligation or debt repayment that targets you (the patron's mark confuses the creditor).

monastic_tradition.corruption_note: Monks follow the patron's general Corruption track; the monastic path does not add a second one. Where a tradition needs its own, it must differ from the general track in kind, not degree.

corruption.benefit: Reveler's Grace: +1 die to social rolls in feasts or crowds.
corruption.cost: Compulsive Toast: Must drink or mark 1 Fatigue when drink is offered.

corruption.benefit: Horned Vitality: Ignore the first 1 Fatigue each scene.
corruption.cost: Restless Appetite: –1 die when abstaining from indulgence (food, drink, or touch).

corruption.benefit: Revel-Kin: Once/scene, summon a minor revel-spirit (advantage die) — a satyr, a maenad, or a muse of seduction.
corruption.cost: Masked Self: Cannot act without a role or guise; –1 die to plain sincerity.

corruption.benefit: Bacchic Fury: Once/session, frenzy grants +2 dice to melee for one exchange. Also, once per scene, ignore the effects of a single social faux pas (the revel covers it).
corruption.cost: Ecstatic Blindness: –1 die to perception outside the revel; you may not notice threats that require sobriety.

corruption.benefit: Feast Without End: Once/session, allies in Near clear all Fatigue.
corruption.cost: Hungering Host: You consume twice as much; denial causes Harm 1 (Stress). You may also develop a reputation: every feast you attend ends in scandal.

corruption.benefit: Satyr King's Mantle: For one scene, become an avatar of revels; all allies gain +2 dice, enemies suffer –2 dice. Your presence also inspires desire: once during the scene, compel one target to act on a hidden passion (Resolve DV 4).
corruption.cost: Tyrant of Pleasure: Mark +3 Obligation; the revel grows monstrous, demanding a sacrifice (an oath, a relationship, or a life). Beast of Endless Revel: Permanent transformation — your mortal form becomes optional; must make Presence+Performance (DV 4) to appear civilized or risk terrifying (or entrancing) all who see you into joining your eternal celebration. You are always at least mildly intoxicated, and sobriety causes you physical pain (1 Fatigue per hour).

rivalries.description: Thrysos opens doors; the Sealed Gate closes them. The reveler seeks to break boundaries and cross thresholds; the gatekeeper seeks to contain and control. Their followers are natural opposites, and their conflicts are often explosive.

Thrysos demands expression; the Silent Choir teaches restraint. The reveler sings; the choir keeps secrets. Their followers rarely see eye to eye — and when they do, it is often at the end of a long night.

playstyle_notes.description: Thrysos turns celebration into courage, influence, and dangerous release. Give the feast people with reasons to attend and reasons to leave. Corruption makes stopping harder even after pleasure has gone. Intrusions can demand one more dance when the follower owes someone a sober promise, or bring consequences from a night the character remembers differently from everyone else.
emphasizes: Ecstatic Release: music, dance, intoxication, the shedding of inhibition (and clothing)
Masked Freedom: identity as performance, the thrill of the anonymous encounter
Feast and Famine: excess, appetite, lust, and the cost of indulgence
Ritual Frenzy: communal ecstasy that transforms participants into something feral and beautiful
The Bacchic Dark: the point where pleasure tips into violence, where the revel demands blood
Seduction as Weapon: using desire to manipulate, distract, or destroy

sample_adventure.title: The Revel That Never Ends
sample_adventure.description: A village on the edge of the Mistlands has been celebrating the same harvest festival for three weeks. No one can leave; no one wants to leave. The wine flows without end, the music never stops, and the dancers have begun to forget their own names. The village elder, sober and terrified, begs the party to find the source of the revelry — a mask that was carved from a lightning-struck tree, now worn by the village's most beautiful and most dangerous inhabitant. The mask is Thrysos's gift, and it will not come off until the wearer has danced their way to ecstatic oblivion. The party must break the revel, convince the wearer to remove the mask, or find a way to end the celebration without being swept into the dance themselves. But the music is beautiful, and the wine is very, very good.
sample_adventure.quote: The mask that dances without a wearer, the wine that whispers secrets, the revel that does not end — these are Thrysos's gifts, and they are never free. The price is always a piece of yourself, given willingly. And sometimes, the price is everything.

guises.name: The Twice-Welcomed Guest
guises.note: His horned image is brought in for the public festival and out again for the smaller feast after the formal audience leaves. The second company disputes what the first performance was permitted to say. Some actors keep the same mask for both occasions, making a patron hear their own praise in a less comfortable voice.

guises.name: The Green Host
guises.note: A noble lends a hall to the Horned Circle and expects an evening's release from rank. The servants still prepare the food and carry away the cups. An observance that permits the lord to be mocked but leaves everyone else at work has released less than it announces. Some hosts discover too late that the revelers noticed.

guises.name: The Storm-Dancer
guises.note: Drums and feet keep time against the wind outside. Participation is valued for the willingness to be seen joining, not because the people are fearless. A person sick with nerves can be welcomed into the dance. One who wishes to stop may find the company's encouragement difficult to distinguish from a command.

guises.name: The Revel-King
guises.note: His sign is painted on a cup passed among crews who cannot be trusted together at a sober negotiation. Temporary fellowship can survive the night and sometimes does. It can also put tomorrow's betrayal within easy reach of someone who learned exactly whom a rival loves while everyone was singing.

guises.name: The Unbounded Guest
guises.note: The familiar title is also used of Mab, but these gatherings honor Thrysos through interruption, shared rhythm, and the loosening of ordinary sequence. Mab's welcome is a different authority. A keeper who invites either by a title alone should know which observance they are opening; the guests need not agree that the mistake was slight.

provenance.origin: An old reveling cult whose public festivals and less governable gatherings have repeatedly exchanged places.
provenance.summary: Thepyric histories preserve civic performances beside accounts of a horned guest who would not remain within the appointed hour. After Astroegro's fall, performance households could carry a mask and songs when they could not carry a sanctuary. Their descendants disagree over whether the restrained civic celebration is a domesticated revel or the private gathering a departure from an older discipline.
provenance.the_migration: Actors, musicians, sailors, and hosts carried observances between ports. A company might be hired because its foreign festival was fashionable and discover that local people heard a different possibility in its temporary freedoms. Noble sponsors adopted the masks and tried to decide who could wear them. Waterfront gatherings dispensed with some formalities while developing their own fierce expectations about who must join.
provenance.why_it_took: The Horned Circle's divisions are not simply sober authority against joyful liberation. A licensed festival can protect performers who could not safely speak outside it; its boundaries can also ensure nothing changes after the masks come off. An unlicensed gathering can create real solidarity and become intolerant of the person who will not surrender themselves to it. Thrysos has room for both feast and frenzy.
provenance.note: Do not turn intoxication, erotic play, or violent ecstasy into compulsory player participation. A cult may exert pressure within the fiction; the table still controls its boundaries. The historical practices of a real reveling religion do not establish consent rules for this fictional Patron.

philosophy.name: Who Is Free at the Feast
philosophy.summary: Thrysos offers a shared release from the selves people are required to perform. The company can make that release another required performance.
philosophy.the_point: A person may want to be carried by a song without surrendering the right to step outside it. The host who cannot bear an empty place in the dance has begun confusing everybody's joy with their own authority over the gathering.
philosophy.the_third_thing: What remains afterward matters. A night that makes an impossible friendship possible has changed something. A night whose least powerful guests must suffer the consequences alone has distributed release unevenly.
philosophy.at_the_table: Give a festival a host, people doing the work, and a consequence that survives morning. A genuine revelation or attachment can emerge without requiring every reveler to lose control. Let leaving, staying, and interrupting carry different possibilities.
